newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Chirac calls on Czechs to share vision of Europe.
newsitem.headline: Chirac calls on Czechs to share vision of Europe.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac on Thursday pledged French support for the Czechs' integration into Western structures and called on them to share his vision of a united Europe with a common security system but also a soul.

Chirac, on the second day of a two-day state visit to Prague, told a joint session of both houses of parliament France would do all it could to support Czech admission to the European Union in 2000 and to NATO in 1999.
"I am not addressing a country which is a candidate for a more or less distant membership. I am addressing the Czech people who tomorrow will be our partner in the great European family," he said.

Chirac, who has visited Hungary, Romania and Poland to underline his support for East Europe's integration with the West, said the process had to go further and that only a united Europe could be a true global power.
"Europe cannot exist in future if it is not reunited," he told a news conference, adding old divisions had to be erased.

"Europe will only be a great power, probably the first, in tomorrow's world if it is united. That presupposes the completion of a European Union of 26 or 27 and the security architecture which will allow us to live without anxiety," he said.
But Chirac said Europe could not ignore the social dimension. "To be truly accepted by our peoples, Europe must have a soul," he said.
The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are seen as the leading candidates to be the next new members of the EU and North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).

But Czech leaders, particularly Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus with whom Chirac held talks on Thursday, have more frequently stressed the economic benefits of Europe as a market than any vision of deeper integration akin to Chirac's.

Czech politicians have also expressed concern at Chirac's insistence that NATO reach a new security relationship with Russia, which bitterly opposes the alliance's eastward expansion plans, before accepting new members.
Chirac told parliament that if accepted into NATO the Czechs would have to play a full role in European defence.
He also reiterated a call for Romania to be invited to join NATO in the first wave after July's Madrid summit and said the Czech Republic and Hungary saw this as desirable.
He added that internal reform of NATO, vital if France is to return to the alliance's military wing after more than 30 years absence, could be completed in time for the summit.

Paris wants a European officer to take over from an American at the head of NATO's Naples-based Southern Command if it is to return to the military wing, which it quit in 1966, but Washington has refused.
"If NATO reform allows a European to assume responsibility which would allow a European defence identity to be defined, France is disposed to join," Chirac said.

"If by contrast, for reasons which I understand perfectly and pose no problems between the United States and France, the Americans plan to keep complete mastery of NATO, France will stay in its present situation," he said.
Earlier, Chirac, who was due to end his visit later on Thursday, told French and Czech business leaders there had to be more French investment in the Czech Republic.
